To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the rate of operant lever-pressing behavior is enhanced by the presentation of a prereward stimulus that is associated with a food pellet, but not by the presentation of an unpaired stimulus or of an unsignaled, food-pellet reinforcer.
a 20-second prereward click/flash stimulus functioned as a conditional accelerator of lever pressing that was being inhibited by a differential-rein-forcement-of-low-rate (DRL) schedule.
a prereward stimulus can function as an external disinhibition of temporally spaced responding.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of stimuli that precede the delivery of food pellets on the rates of lever pressing.
the role of prereward stimuli in the control of operant behavior.

two types of behavioral processes that are related to the effects of stimuli that precede the delivery of reinforcers: (1) the effects of stimuli on operant behavior, and (2) the effects of reinforcers on the behavioral functions of stimuli.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
prereward stimuli function as both external disinhibitors and conditional reinforcers.
the prereward, neutral stimulus functioned as a disinhibitory stimulus that was effective in increasing lever-pressing rates because of a reduction of the inhibition of the lever-pressing response.
the prereward stimuli were effective as external disinhibitors of the response that had been inhibited, and that this inhibition was a function of the schedule.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
prereward stimuli can function as external disinhibitors of operant responding that has been conditioned by prior training under a differential-reward schedule.
a stimulus that is not contingent upon responding can function as an external disinhibition of that response if the response has been previously inhibited by the constraints on the schedule.

a variety of events, some neutral, some reinforcing, and some neither neutral nor reinforcing, can act as external disinhibitors of operant behavior that has been suppressed by the constraints of a schedule.
The main takeaway from our work is that

operant responding is subject to external disinhibitory control by prereward stimuli, and that this control is not limited to the prereward stimuli that are associated with response-independent reinforcers.
the prereward click/flash stimulus was a powerful reinforcer, and that its effects on operant responding were due to its function as an external disinibrator of lever pressing.
the effects of a prereward stimulus can be dissociated from the effects of the reinforcer itself, and that these effects can be attributed to external disinhibitory influences.
